title: Red, and the carpenter's fine peg
hookLine: somebody's paint goes across your half of the wall. what do you see first?
carry: see red as red, then set a fine peg
tomorrow: can a stained mind ever come clean?
last: YELLOW: IN THE SEEN, JUST THE SEEN.

cards: A text arrives in all caps. A car brakes hard in front of you. Somebody's paint goes straight across your half of the wall.
Each time, the body has decided something before the mind catches up: heat in the face, a tight jaw. Yesterday's question was what you see first, red or the story about red.
Buddhaghosa's red disc is built to slow that down. A tray of red flowers, or a red cloth, and the plain word: red, red. Not stop.

teach.b: Red carries a lot of stories: stop signs, warning lights, hearts, a face flushed with anger. The disc asks you to take it without any of them, as one more color in the light. That's the training.

teach.h: WHEN THE STORY HAS ALREADY WON.
teach.b: Then the tradition hands you a second tool, for the moment when the story has already won.
In a sutta about distracting thoughts, the Buddha says: when a thought tied to hate keeps coming back, turn the mind to a different sign, a wholesome one.

teach.h: A FINE PEG KNOCKS OUT A COARSE ONE.
teach.b: He compares it to a carpenter knocking out a coarse peg with a fine one. You don't yank the old peg out with your fingers. You set a better one against it and tap.

teach.h: FIRST THE COLOR, THEN THE PEG.
teach.b: First, red as red: see what's actually there. A streak of paint. A short text.
Second, the fine peg: one true thing that pushes the story out. She's been my friend for years. He's probably scared, not cruel.
Neither move says the anger was wrong, or that nobody did anything. The streak is still on the wall. What changes is who's holding the brush next.
And here's a sentence for the dinner table: the color isn't the fight.

how: In Theravada meditation the red kasina uses red flowers, cloth or other red material, noted as 'red, red'; the carpenter's peg from the Vitakkasanthana Sutta (MN 20) is taught as a way to meet thoughts of hate or craving.

o: the color of anger, studied to learn where rage comes from
a color held as plain color, without the stories it carries
a warning sign that the mind is getting overexcited

games.q: two moves for a red moment — tap the pairs.
p: the plain word for the disc
a wholesome sign set against it

s: the red disc is meant to stir up energy or passion
it's taken as plain color, red, red, without the stories red usually carries.
the Buddha compared changing a thought to a carpenter knocking out a coarse peg with a fine one
you don't yank the bad thought out; you set a better one against it.
swapping in a kind thought means pretending nothing happened
the streak is still on the wall. the fine peg changes what you do next, not what happened.

games.q: your mom snaps at you over dinner after a long shift, and you feel the heat rise. what's the fine peg?
o: snap back once, so it's even, and then let the whole thing go.
remember she's been on her feet all day, and answer gently.
go quiet and stay quiet until she's the one who apologizes.
games.why: the fine peg is one true, kind thought set against the angry one. it doesn't say she was right; it changes what you do next.

practice: Find something red and rest your eyes on it for a few breaths, just the color. Then bring to mind one small irritation from this week and say to yourself, plainly, only what was seen or heard.
Last, set one true, kind thing about that person against it, the way a carpenter sets a fine peg against a coarse one.

wordCard.voice: Red: lohita in Pali. A color with many stories hung on it, held for once as only a color.

orig.note: Pali: red. The color disc held in mind with the plain word, red, red.

carryVoice: The line for today: see red as red, then set a fine peg against the angry thought. Day twelve of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the red kasina: red flowers, cloth or other red material, as with the blue; noted as 'red, red')

Majjhima Nikaya 20 (Vitakkasanthana Sutta: when unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, hate or delusion arise, attend to another sign connected with what is wholesome, as a skilled carpenter knocks out a coarse peg with a fine one)
